\chapter{The Ones That Never Came Back}
\label{ch:ka-ulidavu}
\hlchaptermodality{81}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can recognise every Kannada character this book taught early and then never asked for again, sorted by what kind of thing it is.}

From cold: name all ten consonants, place each in the row of the mouth that makes it, and identify the palatal nasal the book has not printed since the chapter that taught it.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[neladalli]{(\kn{ಾ} \kn{ಿ} \kn{ೆ} \kn{ೊ} \kn{ೋ} \kn{ೃ} \kn{ಂ} \kn{ಃ}) — eight that cannot stand alone}

\label{lesson:KA-R81-signs-that-hang}



\begin{quote}
Two of these you met in the book's first handful of pages. Name the one that lengthens a vowel, and the one that makes it \emph{i}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script: six signs and two marks}
Six vowel signs, cold. Each attaches to a consonant and replaces the \emph{a} built into it:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{sign} & \textbf{sound} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\kn{ಾ}} & \emph{ā} \\
\textbf{\kn{ಿ}} & \emph{i} \\
\textbf{\kn{ೆ}} & \emph{e} \\
\textbf{\kn{ೊ}} & \emph{o} \\
\textbf{\kn{ೋ}} & \emph{ō} \\
\textbf{\kn{ೃ}} & \emph{ṛ} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The last is the odd one. \textbf{\kn{ೃ}} writes a vowel that behaves like a consonant in the mouth, inherited from Sanskrit and rare enough that a reader can go pages without meeting it — which is exactly why it is here.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Two marks now, and they are not vowel signs at all.

Read these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಂ}} — say what it adds to the syllable it follows
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಃ}} — say the same for this one
  \item \textbf{\kn{ೊ}} and \textbf{\kn{ೋ}} back to back, and say what separates them
\end{itemize}

\textbf{\kn{ಂ}} and \textbf{\kn{ಃ}} ride \emph{after} a syllable rather than reshaping its vowel. That is the division worth keeping: a vowel sign changes the sound already there, a mark adds one behind it.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the eight writes a vowel that acts like a consonant? (\textbf{\kn{ೃ}}.) Which two follow a syllable instead of reshaping it? (\textbf{\kn{ಂ}} and \textbf{\kn{ಃ}}.) And which one only makes the vowel longer? (\textbf{\kn{ಾ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nintiruva]{(\kn{ಇ} \kn{ಈ} \kn{ಉ} \kn{ಊ} \kn{ಓ}) — five that need nothing to lean on}

\label{lesson:KA-R81-vowels-that-stand}



\begin{quote}
Two full-size letters, not signs. Name the one that says \emph{i} and the one that says \emph{u}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script: the same vowel, two shapes}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{standing letter} & \textbf{sound} & \textbf{when you use it} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\kn{ಇ}} & \emph{i} & the word opens on the vowel \\
\textbf{\kn{ಈ}} & \emph{ī} & the same, held long \\
\textbf{\kn{ಉ}} & \emph{u} & the word opens on the vowel \\
\textbf{\kn{ಊ}} & \emph{ū} & the same, held long \\
\textbf{\kn{ಓ}} & \emph{ō} & the word opens on the vowel \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Every one of these has a partner among the signs. The difference is not the sound — it is \textbf{whether a consonant is there to carry it.} A vowel with nothing in front of it must be written full-size; the moment a consonant arrives, the same vowel shrinks to a sign hanging off it.

Two pairs make this visible: \textbf{\kn{ಇ}} against \textbf{\kn{ಿ}}, and \textbf{\kn{ಓ}} against \textbf{\kn{ೋ}}. Same vowel, twice, and the shape tells you where in the word you are.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Read these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಈ}} and \textbf{\kn{ಊ}} — say which is the long one in each pair
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಾ}} — and say why this one has no standing partner among the five
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What decides whether a vowel is written full-size or as a sign? (\textbf{Whether a consonant is there to carry it.}) Name the standing letter that pairs with \textbf{\kn{ೋ}}. (\textbf{\kn{ಓ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hattu]{(\kn{ಕ} \kn{ಗ} \kn{ಚ} \kn{ಝ} \kn{ಞ} \kn{ಥ} \kn{ಪ} \kn{ಯ} \kn{ಸ} \kn{ಹ}) — ten, gathered at last}

\label{lesson:KA-R81-ten-consonants}



\begin{quote}
Two that differ by voice alone. Read \textbf{\kn{ಕ}}, then \textbf{\kn{ಗ}}, and say what your throat does on the second that it did not do on the first.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script: ten, sorted by where they are made}
These ten arrived one per chapter, scattered from the book's opening to well past its middle, and no page ever put them side by side. Sorted by the mouth rather than by the order you met them:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{where} & \textbf{letters} \\
\midrule
\textbf{throat} & \textbf{\kn{ಕ}} \emph{ka} · \textbf{\kn{ಗ}} \emph{ga} \\
\textbf{palate} & \textbf{\kn{ಚ}} \emph{ca} · \textbf{\kn{ಝ}} \emph{jha} · \textbf{\kn{ಞ}} \emph{ña} \\
\textbf{teeth} & \textbf{\kn{ಥ}} \emph{tha} \\
\textbf{lips} & \textbf{\kn{ಪ}} \emph{pa} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Read down the middle row. \textbf{\kn{ಚ}}, \textbf{\kn{ಝ}} and \textbf{\kn{ಞ}} are made in the same place, and they differ only in voice, breath and nasality — which is the organising idea the whole Kannada consonant grid is built on.

\textbf{\kn{ಞ}} is the one to look at twice. It is the nasal of the palatal row and is rare on the page; a reader who has not seen it since the chapter that taught it will not place it at all.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Three that belong to no stop row, and one more from above.

Read these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಯ}} — a glide, not a stop
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಸ}} — the hiss
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಹ}} — the breath, and the letter your first \emph{yes} opens on
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಥ}} — and say which row it belongs to
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the ten is the palatal nasal? (\textbf{\kn{ಞ}}.) Which pair differs by voice alone? (\textbf{\kn{ಕ}} and \textbf{\kn{ಗ}}.) And which one opens the word for \emph{yes}? (\textbf{\kn{ಹ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
